captions.instagram:
How does a CT scanner work?

A CT scanner spins an X-ray tube around you three times a second, takes about a thousand shadows each turn, and a computer turns them into slices of your body. Take one apart in 3D, then rebuild a slice yourself with real maths.

→ A CT scanner is a doughnut that spins an X-ray tube and a curved detector around you.
→ Slip rings let the ring keep spinning, about three times every second.
→ Each angle casts a shadow; stacked together they make a striped sinogram.
→ In a helical scan the table glides through while the tube spins, tracing a spiral.
→ Smear every shadow back across the picture and a blurry, streaky slice appears.

youtubeLong.title: How does a CT scanner work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A CT scanner spins an X-ray tube around you three times a second, takes about a thousand shadows each turn, and a computer turns them into slices of your body. Take one apart in 3D, then rebuild a slice yourself with real maths.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/ctscanclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/ctscanclear

In this video:
• A spinning ring of X-rays. Inside the doughnut-shaped gantry, a heavy disc carries an X-ray tube and a curved detector with 64 or more rows of sensors.
• Hundreds of shadows, one slice. Each detector measures how much X-ray got through along one line.
• Rebuilding the picture. Smear every shadow back across the image and add them up: back-projection.
• Every pixel is a number. CT measures attenuation and reports it in Hounsfield units: water is 0, air is −1000, fat about −100, bone +400 to over +1000.
• Dose and speed. A head CT gives about 2 mSv, a chest CT about 7 and an abdomen and pelvis CT about 8 to 10, against about 2.4 mSv a year from nature and 0.02 to 0.1 for a chest X-ray.
• Modern tricks. Dual-energy CT uses two X-ray energies to tell materials apart, like uric acid and calcium kidney stones.
